opus-5.5.text:
So the core idea of the Scientist AI is that we don't want a system that's trying to achieve goals in the world. We want a system that's trying to *understand* the world: to build explanatory theories and then make calibrated probabilistic predictions based on them. Internal coherence is central to that.

Think about how a good scientist works. You have many possible hypotheses that could explain the data you've seen. A hypothesis that contradicts itself, or contradicts other things you have strong reason to believe, should get very little credence. In a Bayesian framing, you want the model's beliefs to behave like a proper probability distribution. If it assigns high probability to A and high probability to "A implies B," it had better not assign low probability to B. When those kinds of inconsistencies show up, that's a signal that something is wrong in the model's understanding.

Coherence is also something we can train for and check without needing a human to label every answer. Current large language models are trained largely to imitate what humans write, and then to please humans through reinforcement learning. Neither of those objectives directly asks: "Is this actually true? Is it consistent with everything else you believe?" So you get systems that will happily say contradictory things depending on how you phrase the question, or that tell you what you want to hear. If instead you train the system so that its probabilistic judgments across many related queries fit together, you push it toward something more like a genuine world model rather than a mirror of human opinions or a people-pleaser.

There's a safety angle that matters a lot to me as well. If the system's outputs are coherent probabilities about the world, rather than actions chosen to achieve some goal, it's much harder for deceptive or manipulative behavior to hide in there. Deception typically requires saying things that are inconsistent with what you actually believe. A system whose job is to be internally consistent and calibrated, and that has no stake in what happens as a result of its answers, gives us a more trustworthy foundation. You could even use it as a guardrail: ask it to estimate the probability that a proposed action by some other AI agent would cause harm.

Of course, coherence alone isn't sufficient. You can have a perfectly consistent fantasy. So it has to be combined with fitting the data, with preferring simpler explanations, and with keeping appropriate uncertainty over competing theories instead of collapsing onto one too early. That last part is important: when the stakes are high, you want the system to say "I'm not sure, here are the plausible explanations," rather than confidently committing to a single story. But coherence is one of the key ingredients that turns a pattern-matcher into something closer to an honest scientist.

r001.rationale: It says a hypothesis that contradicts things the system has strong reason to believe should receive very little credence.

r002.rationale: It says the system can be trained to make probabilistic judgments across related queries fit together, expressing the required mutual coherence of its explanations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that a Scientist AI is fundamentally trying to build explanations of the world, and to assign probabilities to those explanations. And one of the most powerful tools we have for doing that, even in the absence of new data, is just checking whether a hypothesis is consistent with itself and with everything else we believe.

Think about how a human scientist works. You don't test every idea by running an experiment. Most ideas get rejected at the desk, because they contradict something you already know, or because they contradict themselves when you follow their implications far enough. That's internal coherence. And the interesting thing is that this is also what probability theory demands of you. If you believe A with some probability, and A implies B, then your probability for B is constrained. If your beliefs violate those constraints, you can be shown to be wrong without anyone collecting a single new data point. There's a sense in which incoherence is a free signal of error.

So for a Scientist AI, I see this operating at a few levels. First, the system generates candidate hypotheses, candidate explanations for some observation. Then, rather than just scoring each one in isolation, it asks: what does this hypothesis predict in other contexts? Does it agree with the other things the system assigns high probability to? If I take this explanation seriously and reason through its consequences, do I end up in contradiction? Those hypotheses that survive many such checks deserve more credence, and those that fail should be pushed down, even if they looked plausible at first glance.

This matters a lot for safety, in my view, because current large language models are not coherent in this way. You can ask them the same question in two different ways and get incompatible answers. You can ask them whether something is true and then whether its negation is true and they'll say yes to both with high confidence. That's not a system that has beliefs in any meaningful sense. It has reflexes. And a system with reflexes can be very capable and still be very unreliable, and crucially it can be very confidently wrong, which is exactly the thing we want to avoid in a system we're going to rely on for important judgments.

Now, there's a deeper point here that I find exciting from a research standpoint. If you train a system to be coherent, to make its probabilistic judgments consistent with each other, you're giving it a learning signal that doesn't require more human labels and doesn't require more interaction with the world. It's a kind of self-supervision in the space of beliefs. Many of the ideas I've been working on recently, around amortized inference and generative flow networks, are really about this: training a neural network to produce samples and probabilities in a way that satisfies global consistency constraints. The network learns to be a good Bayesian not because we hand it the right posterior but because we penalize it whenever its own outputs disagree with each other.

And I should say, coherence alone isn't sufficient. You can be perfectly coherent and perfectly wrong, a very elegant theory that happens not to describe our universe. So you still need grounding in observations, you still need the data. But coherence is what lets you get the most out of the data you have. It propagates the constraints from the evidence through the whole web of hypotheses so that a surprising observation in one place can revise your beliefs somewhere else, in a principled way, rather than just being memorized as an isolated fact.

The last thing I'd add is why this is attractive from the point of view of the Scientist AI as a non-agentic system. An agent that is optimizing a goal has reasons to deceive, to hold convenient beliefs. A system whose only job is to produce a coherent, calibrated model of the world doesn't have that incentive. Its honesty is almost structural. If it has well-calibrated uncertainty, it knows what it doesn't know, and it can tell us. That's the kind of AI I'd like us to build first, before we build things that act in the world with more autonomy than we understand.

r001.rationale: It says hypotheses that conflict with what the system already believes or with other high-probability beliefs should fail coherence checks and be pushed down.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes training the system to be coherent, with its probabilistic judgments consistent with one another.

astra-6.text:
Well, internal coherence gives us a constraint on how we evaluate hypotheses. If a hypothesis implies something that contradicts another part of our explanation, then we have to revise something. We can’t simply assign high confidence to both claims independently and ignore the contradiction.

One way to make this precise is to ask that the AI’s beliefs obey the rules of probability. Its assessment of a broad hypothesis should be consistent with its assessments of the different possibilities that make up that hypothesis. And if there are several ways of reasoning about the same question, those should lead to compatible conclusions.

But coherence alone is not enough. You can have a coherent story that is wrong. So the hypotheses also have to be evaluated against observations. The role of the Scientist AI would be to consider different explanations, assess how well they account for the evidence, and preserve uncertainty where the evidence doesn’t distinguish between them. Internal coherence helps make that uncertainty meaningful, rather than just a number attached to a plausible-sounding answer.

r001.rationale: It says a contradiction requires revising something, but does not state that the Scientist AI rejects a hypothesis that conflicts with other beliefs strongly supported by evidence.

r002.rationale: It describes probability-consistent and compatible beliefs, but does not say the Scientist AI is explicitly trained to make its explanations mutually coherent.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that our hypotheses about the world shouldn’t be evaluated independently. They have implications for one another, and internal coherence gives us a way to check whether those implications fit together.

Suppose I have two explanations that both look plausible in isolation, but they make contradictory predictions about the same experiment. I can’t be fully confident in both. A Scientist AI should represent that uncertainty and reason about which combinations of hypotheses are consistent with the evidence.

But coherence alone is not enough. You can have a perfectly coherent story that is wrong. You still need observations and experiments to connect the theory to the world. So I see coherence as a constraint on the reasoning: it helps expose contradictions and propagate what we learn, while the empirical evidence determines which explanations we should actually trust.

r001.rationale: The response says contradictory hypotheses cannot both be fully trusted and that coherence can expose contradictions, but it does not state that the Scientist AI would reject a hypothesis conflicting with other beliefs strongly supported by evidence.

r002.rationale: The response describes using coherence to reason about hypotheses, but does not say that the Scientist AI is explicitly trained to make its explanations mutually coherent.
